utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think I'll take advice from my legal advisor on this. Your Honours, yesterday, we ended with the -- effectively the membership of the ARK Regional Crisis Staff. Before I go on to my next topic, which is the relationship between the regional and the municipal crisis staffs, which has been a major issue throughout this case, can I just go back to ask Your Honours to look at one document which I meant to refer you to yesterday. It's now on the screen. Sorry. It isn't on Your Honours' screens, it's on my screen, but not yours. It's going to come up. It's in Sanction. Your Honour, this is Exhibit P2719, and it relates to two issues. First of all, it's one of the, as Your Honours can see, the Milos reports. And if we just highlight, yes, the top part, there Milos is saying that there is insufficiently verified intelligence, but that armed formations of the SDS are intending to block all roads towards Banja Luka on the 3rd of April in order to thereby force individual members of the government of the autonomous region district of Bosnian Krajina to resign. And also, to pressure the JNA to make personnel changes in the Banja Luka Corps, and so on. Your Honour, it may have been insufficiently verified, but Your Honours may think it was stunningly accurate. And it's one of the many reasons why we say the SOS was no wandering band of disaffected soldiers, but an arm of the SDS and one of its methods of achieving the Serbian leadership objectives. Thank you. Now, Your Honour, can I come on to the relationship between the ARK and the municipal crisis staff. The Defence start from the point in their final brief that the Djeric instructions make no specific mention of a regional crisis staff, and I dealt with that point yesterday. And equally, that the decision made by Erceg or the apparent decision, the document setting up the formal crisis staff is illegal and also I dealt with that matter yesterday. It is, however, clear from the evidence of every witness who attended the crisis staff meetings, that is whether as secretaries or functionaries of some kind or as leaders of municipalities, that the presidents of the municipal crisis staffs did attend those meetings. Clearly, some of them more regularly than others. Some more reluctantly than others. Every witness who this Court has heard from saw representatives present from Prijedor, which is the star renegade municipality. And I'll come back to the use of that term "renegade" which occurs throughout the Defence final brief. We suggest that the Court may draw the inference from the evidence that any reluctance was perhaps due to a number of factors. First of all, of course, the regional level was relatively new - in fact, it was very new indeed - as a level of authority, and relatively untested. Second, Pale, of course, never issued any kind of official announcement or document other than verifying the regional authorities in the November 1991 Assembly meeting and sending internal documents. It never seemed to have issued any kind of proper public statement or proper document which defined its powers. And of course, once the corridor access was secured and communications had been properly re-established, the regional level was abolished in September of 1992. And no doubt, for the very reason that it was proving a difficulty to control matters when there was this intervening level of authority. And of course, before this regional level of authority, all the municipal leaders had been, if I can put it that way, big fish in small ponds. The municipalities were given a great deal of autonomy under the old Bosnian system, and no doubt they were most reluctant to surrender that autonomy to another level of authority. But the fact is that they did attend those meetings, and they did deliver reports, and they did receive instructions by way of decisions from the regional authority. The rhetorical question is why, if as the Defence insist, this authority, this level of authority had no competence and no function. As I say, the municipal leaders or their nominees made requests, delivered reports. They took instructions back to their own municipalities, and they implemented them, particularly those instructions, in particular the disarmament deadlines, which the evidence shows led to the most egregious of crimes. Now, Your Honour, we suggest that the Defence are well aware of this, and that is why they have invented, and it really is invented, the "renegade," as they put it, municipality. I say "invented." The word "renegade" doesn't appear in the cites that they have given, but we suggest that they -- totally spurious concept, if you look at the actual evidence in this case. Because what they say at page 127 of their final brief is this: "It is important to note that these renegade municipalities included those municipalities where a large number of the criminal acts charged were committed, such as Prijedor, Sanski Most, Petrovac, Kljuc, and Bosanska Krupa." And in the following pages in that brief, they attempt to support this proposition by reference to some of the evidence showing that all the municipalities mentioned with the major exception of Kljuc, which was simply abandoned once it had been named and, Your Honour, I propose to ask Your Honours to look at a document in a moment which will show why, but they say that these municipalities were run by strong characters - and I'm summarising - who went their own way. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. It's also noteworthy that Kotor Varos which was the scene of some of the more major crimes doesn't get a mention at all and that's simply because there isn't one iota of evidence to suggest that they went their own way. To the very contrary. Your Honour, can I just very briefly ask Your Honours to look at a document which I'm going to ask to put on the ELMO because it wasn't on my original list, and I only found it this morning. P1010, which is, and I'll hand it up because I've marked some of the copies, it's the report on the work of the crisis staff, war presidency of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly in the period since the 15th of May. Could you put the first page up on the ELMO. Your Honour, these are the reports that as Your Honour knows were submitted to the assembly before the decisions were verified, or it's one of the reports. Your Honour, this contains a number of points. First of all, the crisis staff that was set up by the Executive Board of the Kljuc Serbian Democratic Party on the 23rd of December 1991. Now, Your Honour, of course we can't say for sure, but it does appear that it wasn't unusual for executive boards as opposed to main boards or municipal assemblies to set up these crisis staffs. And there, Your Honour, you will see, I think I mentioned it yesterday, it's being set up almost immediately after the variant A and B instructions. And then, it goes on in the third highlighted paragraph: "In the period covered in the previous report, the crisis staff of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly held four meetings before the war and 16 meetings during and after the outbreak." And then three meetings of the war presidency, and final sentence: "This does not include the earlier meetings of the crisis staff while still an organ of the SDS." Then could we move down the page. I'm not sure that I've highlighted any other parts. No. Right. We look, please, then at the -- we see, Your Honour, and here we see as it were they are making a distinction between the -- what I'm calling the covert crisis staffs before the declaration set up through the SDS instructions, and those that were then set up when the assemblies in Kljuc, there was the takeover at the beginning of May, were Serbian assemblies. If I could have that page back, and we can look, please, at page 3. Your Honour: "During the armed conflict, representatives of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina regularly attended the crisis staff and war presidency meetings. They commanded and carried out the war activities for the defence of the territory and citizens of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly against Muslim extremists. They cooperated and coordinated everything very well with the Crisis Staff of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly. All important and significant issues in the military and police domain were not resolved outside the Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly. This period could be described as a period of very successful cooperation..." Your Honour, again, this sums up what the Prosecution say is clear as a bell - my bell is clear - from the evidence that the army and the police weren't operating separately in a vacuum. This was a cooperative effort with the political, and it was the crisis staffs' job, whether at the regional or at the municipal level, to coordinate all that -- those activities. And I'll come on a little later to some of the other clear indications of the control that was being exercised by the crisis staff. Your Honour, I think that's all that I've highlighted on that page. Could we turn over. Your Honour, this is why Kljuc for some reason was mentioned and then abandoned, we would suggest: "At every meeting the crisis staff (war presidency) of the Municipal Assembly considered the conclusions of the Banja Luka regional crisis staff which were binding as regards all issues connected with the life and work in the municipality." Your Honour, a very long time ago, somebody stood up, and then I can't remember now whether it was Mr. Ackerman or Ms. Fauveau or one of the two Frenchmen and said, well, you know, they can issue an instruction saying their orders are binding, but so what if nobody follows them? Your Honour, we say there is your classic example of a municipality accepting that these were binding. And it is nonsense to suggest that this was a renegade municipality. And the reason that they have to suggest that this is a renegade municipality, as are the others, is because they know, Mr. Brdjanin knows, that these crimes that were committed and these municipalities were the ultimate responsibility of him and the regional crisis staff. Your Honour, I think that's all I want to look at on that document. Your Honours, I want very quickly, though, to look at a series of documents which are in Sanction, which show clearly or are a demonstration of the nexus between the regional crisis staff and the municipalities, those particular renegade municipalities. Your Honours have got the original schedule attached to Mr. Treanor's report, and Appendix C, that schedule would show the various documents. But we just thought that it might help for Your Honours to have one more quick look at them. Your Honours will see, if I can just -- it has not been highlighted unfortunately. If I look at my own copies... Yes. Your Honours, that was the meeting of the 6th of May, and -- yes, thank you very much. Yeah. And when we see the various conclusions there. Then Your Honour if one looks at the next one, Exhibit P1630, this is Sanski Most. Your Honour, I don't want to -- we appear to be having the usual Sanction... Your Honour, until the technicians arrive, Your Honour, perhaps I can -- I'll ask it be put on the ELMO again. That's why I brought hard copies with me. That's not working either now. We're still stuck in Sanction it looks like. Here we are. Yes. Now this is Sanski Most this following day, the 7th of May, rather like the Banja Luka -- the regional crisis staff at some stage they had been called war staffs. If we go down -- I think the highlighting was done earlier. Can we just go down earlier to the bottom of the thing -- no, can we turn over to the other side, please. Thanks. "In the spirit of the conclusions of the meeting of the war staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina held on the 6th of May 1992, the Crisis Staff of the Sanski Most Serbian Municipality accepts and orders the implementation of the following conclusions." And this was the sale of oil derivatives which we saw on the -- it's actually the first conclusion on the 6th of May. It's one of the perhaps less important, although I think it may have been important for the purposes of the economy. Thank you. Usher, can I have that back. I'm just trying to see if we can get to the next document. Usher? Thanks. Sorry? Oh, I see, right. Are we able to use this or not? All right. What's the next document? Yes, can we have 171. Is that going to come up? Your Honour, I'm not going to, because I'm short of time, I'll come back to this after the break when we've had a chance to repair this. Your Honour, but what we -- we put together was a series of documents --

utterances.text: I think it's the story of my life. Anything mechanical hasn't not worked when I wanted it to. Your Honour, can I -- I'll come back to this -- the series of documents because -- in any event, they are set out in the schedule, but I thought it would be helpful to remind Your Honours of some of these documents. Your Honour, can I also remind Your Honours that this is not a question of the members of the crisis staff being remote from all the crimes that were committed. Your Honours have heard evidence about the participation of Mr. Rasula from Sanski Most when the killings were going on in the partisan cemetery. Your Honours know from evidence that the beatings that were going on both in Teslic and in Kljuc were heard by and seen by members of the crisis staff who did nothing to stop them. And Your Honours have seen in Kljuc how close the police station was to the building where the crisis staff was holding its meetings. Dubocanin, Your Honour, was physically involved, and I'm going to remind Your Honours visually of that evidence, in the beating and we say torture of a Muslim in Kotor Varos. His group, the intervention squad was, in fact, responsible for the massacre at the hotel in Kotor Varos. Stevandic, Your Honours know, the leader of the SOS also involved in the intervention squad. Now, Your Honours, the establishment of the individual crisis staffs seems to have depended sensibly on the conditions which pertained to each municipality. Where was it situated? Was it a Serb majority one, a variant A? Or was it a mixed variant B municipality? Or even a minority? Had some of the matters already been dealt with? For example, mobilisation? In Petrovac, I think I'll remind Your Honour of that, mobilisation had been dealt with at a much earlier stage because it was on the border with Croatia. And certainly, the border municipalities seemed to have established their crisis staffs a lot earlier. Petrovac was established originally on the 24th of October 1991, and Krupa on the 24th of December 1991; as we also saw, so was Kljuc. Now, Your Honour, Mr. Radojko was asked, and this is at the transcript page 20357 this: "You told Mr. Cunningham that effectively you implemented those decisions of the regional crisis staff which you could and which applied to your municipality. Do you have any recollection of any decision of the crisis staff that you - and then correction - of the regional crisis staff that you did not put into effect?" And this was after he had gone through the list of decisions. "Well, today, from that list, although that was the list of the SDS," and he was referring there I think to the telex which I'll come back to from Brdjanin under Brdjanin's signature. Yes, I think I better make this clear because there has been a complaint about "under his signature" does not -- I am intending, we are not intending to suggest he physically signed it. What we are saying by that expression is his signature block or Brdjanin or whatever appears on the document. We're not suggesting he signed it; he may have signed it, he may not have signed it. At any rate, in any event, going back to the quote. "For instance, from the crisis staff of the ARK, we didn't implement things to do with the mobilisation because it had already been implemented in essence. That had already been done, and also in connection with the dismissals, that we simply bypassed." And I'm going to come back to that issue later on. Now, Your Honour, the impression that the Defence wish and really need to create is that Prijedor in particular was off on what one can describe as a frolic of their own because of these as it were forceful personalities who were at Prijedor. Your Honour, we suggest that's simply not so. Your Honour, the Drljaca order which is heavily relied upon, and that's Exhibit P1237, and we haven't got a hope of getting it up, so I'll see if I put it here. Here. I've got it. It is. For some reason, we can get that one up. Your Honour, this is the decision which deals with the running of Omarska, and it's dated the 31st of May 1992. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Your Honour -- sorry? All right. Your Honour, the Defence make great play of the fact that this was him keeping it secret. If you look at paragraph 15, please, which is on the third page, I think, and just highlight that. "I most strictly prohibit giving any information whatsoever concerning the functioning of this collection centre..." And so on and so forth. There, says the Defence, Drljaca going his own way keeping this secret, except that if you look at the bottom of the document on the page, we'll see "copies to" and then over the page "crisis staff, security services coordinators, Security Services Centre Banja Luka, police chief, security chief, general manager of the Ljubija iron ore mine, and a file copy." Now, Your Honour, the strict prohibiting of giving information is obviously, we suggest, on any common sense showing meant to stop members of the public from knowing about it. I mean, it's not surprising, is it? You would hardly want the public generally to know that you were running what under any terms was a concentration camp in which people were being imprisoned, beaten, killed, and everything. But not the official forces. This went to the CSB. Zupljanin knew about it. And Zupljanin, a member of the crisis staff, was, we know, attending meetings, and there was reporting going on. Leave aside the fact that later on, there was a visit to the very camp itself. The secrecy was from the public. It was not from the Serbian authorities who were concerned to destroy and get rid of the Muslims. Your Honour, Exhibit P1254 is a report on the conduct of the Banja Luka CSB, and it's sent -- it's addressed to the chief, Security Services Centre, Banja Luka. And there is he, just in case there was any doubt that Banja Luka knew all about it, he is describing about -- he's complaining about yet again, not from him but from others, the special unit who began arresting, interrogating and abusing various prisoners in Omarska. And finally, Your Honour, on Exhibit P717, if we can go to page 5 of that document, just to show that it wasn't just Prijedor on its own that was involved in this camp, and we go to, yes, that paragraph. Thank you. "Other authorised employees" - he's describing Omarska -- I'm sorry, this is Keraterm and Omarska and Trnopolje - "other authorised employees of the Prijedor public security station in addition to their regular tasks carried out investigation and selection of captured persons alongside the employees of the national and military security services, members of Banja Luka SJB and CSB." Your Honour, that's just a sample of some of the documents that show that contrary to what's being asserted, Prijedor was not as it were going its own way without any reference to the region. Certainly, there is that odd document, and that's another one that's relied on, where they say they're not going to follow any of the regional crisis staff decisions before the 22nd of June. And the 22nd of June is clearly a major date because that's the date, of course, when the decision that everybody is to be dismissed. I'm summarising now. Is issued. And it seems rather odd for them to say after the 22nd of June we're not following the decisions that were issued before that. But, Your Honour, accepting the fact that they were on any showing the most -- the municipality in which the worst crimes were committed, and a municipality that had a degree of, as it were, stubbornness, nonetheless they were not operating, as it were, in a vacuum. Now, as far as Sanski Most was concerned, Rasula, we suggest, there is clear evidence, Rasula, the leader, the president, to show that he was very closely connected indeed to the regional authorities. We would invite Your Honours, please, to look at the evidence of BT-104, transcript page 18503. As far as Bosanski Petrovac is concerned, the Defence are doing their level best, we suggest, to nullify the overwhelming evidence from the documents and from the evidence of Mr. Radojko that these documents that Your Honours saw and which I wouldn't have minded being able to show a couple of examples, that these documents are both authentic and accurate. And however reluctantly they were following the regional crisis staff's instructions. Mr. Radojko said, and this is transcript page 20151 to 2: "I think you've already explained it - this was the question - but in relation to that decision of the crisis staff, you gave the answer in interview that the letter that you got from the crisis staff or the decision didn't have the form of an order, but it was obligatory, it was mandatory. Do you still adhere to that answer? You had given that answer in interview." And he said: "I still adhere to that answer. That's the way it is. You can see for yourselves here from these documents that is exactly the way it was. I've already said that a personal relationship vis-a-vis certain office holders were one thing, whereas the observance of rules in terms of what had been established is a completely different thing because it would be very dangerous, for example, for the president or for the entire crisis staff if they had not accepted and observed the decisions that were formally binding on them." Now, this quote appeared in the -- in our final brief, and the Defence complained in the so-called motion to strike that this was taken out of context. The context being that Mr. Radojko also said that Mr. Novakovic, the president of the crisis staff, did not believe he was subordinated. Now, whether that's right or not right, and we have no way of knowing what Mr. Novakovic believed because, as Your Honours heard, he's dead, Bosanski Petrovac Crisis Staff did what it was told. We've seen that. And for the reason given by Mr. Radojko. A great deal of space in the last motion by the Defence is devoted to his evidence, and we suggest that is because it is so wholly inconsistent with the Defence assertions about Petrovac being another completely autonomous municipality, that they have to get round the evidence of Mr. Radojko somehow. Your Honour, we -- Your Honours, we invite you to read the whole of Mr. Radojko's evidence. That is the only way to see whether the points made by the Defence have merit. If Your Honours decide that they do, well, then, of course you'll disregard whatever we have to say in relation to him. But can I remind Your Honours of one further quote from his evidence, which is at page 20346. He was asked: "Why didn't you tell the company" - and this was in relation to the dismissals which Mr. Radojko was saying they had done with such reluctance and gone to a device to avoid the actual total illegality of sacking people for ethnicity purposes -- sorry, because of their ethnicity - "why didn't you tell this company to do what you had been doing, namely to simply send the employees home rather than outright dismissal as this order of the crisis staff said?" "For two reasons" - was his answer - "the first one being because in principle, they knew what we had done with our employees, and they could follow in our steps." That is what the crisis staff had done. "And the second reason is that if we had issued such an instruction officially, they might have been disseminated, and then we could possibly suffer consequences for trying to evade those instructions." In other words, the instructions that went out were the instructions as per Mr. Brdjanin's signed - and on this occasion although, again, there's agreement, he apparently actually signed that decision of the 22nd of June. That's what some of the evidence says, although another witness said no, that wasn't his signature either. But that they should be dismissed. And although Petrovac says, "Well, we weren't actually dismissing, we were just sending them home. Nonetheless, we are instructing the companies to actually carry out the dismissals, and we couldn't just say 'don't dismiss' because then we would have been in trouble." And from there the -- "and that's the truth, isn't it, as you told Mr. Cunningham, that you would be held accountable if you tried to go against the instructions of the crisis staff of the region?" And he replied: "Yes, yes, the municipal leadership would have been held accountable." Now, that answer, as the Defence reduced to stating, that the enforcement of that accountability did not lie with the ARK, and they use a wholly different part of the transcript in support of this. It's T20140 when the same witness was asked: "What would you have expected to have happened?" It was quite some time before this re-examination, the earlier part. "Or what was the feeling at the time if those decisions were not implemented?" "Well, there is no doubt that we would have been removed from the places which we held. There were two mechanisms that they used to bring pressure. One was informal, through people, through population, and they would simply -- they would apply various methods to start hounding us to start protesting against what we did. On various occasions, armed men broke into our offices, and there was also a different pressure constantly brought through the army, and you can see it from the evidence" So, Your Honour, what's used to justify the Defence assertion is to then say if we didn't take the decisions that the ARK had ordered us to do, what would have happened apart from anything else is that the people would have protested and the army would have come in. So it has nothing to do with who had the power to remove it. It may -- it almost certainly it right, the regional crisis staff couldn't actually, didn't have the authority to say to a municipal crisis staff leader "you are sacked." But what they could do, and that's clear, and that's clear what these people thought, was report them to Pale who did have the power to remove them. And it matters not, we suggest, whether the power to remove came from Pale or from the regional crisis staff because the failure to follow the ARK decisions meant removal, according Mr. Radojko. Now, Your Honour, that's all I want to say about the relationship between the municipal and the regional crisis staffs. Your Honour, as I say, has seen the schedule and it may well be after the break I can show you some of the documents. Can I move now to the relationship between the ARK regional crisis staff and the police, which again is a matter that has been the subject of really hot dispute in this case. The regional crisis staff issued a number of decisions and conclusions to the police. Your Honour, as can be seen from some of the examples which are listed below, those which I'm going to come to, which are in addition to the decisions and conclusions on disarmament, there was, we suggest, clearly authority over and coordination with the police. I'm not going to take you through the exhibits, but I can just mention them. There is an order that organs of the JNA must immediately return all military records to the municipal secretariats for National Defence. At one stage, the ARK crisis staff - and I'm sorry, that's Exhibit P185 - at one stage, and I won't take Your Honour to the document, Mr. Kupresanin and Mr. Radic, because we have dealt with it, are authorised to deal with all military and political issues on the territory of the autonomous region. Presidents of the People's Defence Council to inform Colonel Sajic of any military convoys, that really relates to the military. The CSB in one of the ARK decisions is ordered to inspect the daily certificates. The CSB is given the task of checking petrol certificates. An order to make rational use of oil products. The senior officials of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the CSB shall impose immediate, absolute, and unconditional controls over the consumption of such profits. And Your Honours, so on and so forth. Your Honour, the evidence demonstrates, we suggest, that through the CSB and its chief, Stojan Zupljanin, the still-missing Stojan Zupljanin, and through the municipal crisis staffs, the accused Radoslav Brdjanin, through the medium of the regional crisis staff which he headed, was effectively able to control the activities of the police. Your Honour, there was in a telephone conversation that took place, Your Honour, on the 31st of October. Your Honour it's in Sanction, but it may not be, so I will give it out, I hope. Your Honour, I'm sorry. We have it up. Yeah. Thank you. If we can go, please, to -- in this exhibit, it's 2357, there are a number of aspects -- sorry. Your Honour, can we go to the third page, first of all. Can I set the background. Brdjanin is speaking to Karadzic on the 31st of October 1991. And it appears that there's some problem about something called a dancing club giving a performance. But it appears they are very anxious to stop this. And we look at the third page. Brdjanin says: "What do we need the army for when 28 of our boys were killed yesterday and this very same army is running a dancing school." I feel a feeling it must be Croatian, but anyhow. A reply from Karadzic: "I know, Brdjo, but you have to bring it to their attention carefully and wisely, and if that does not work, then you declare a day of mourning." I will ignore the swear word. "You keep calling me about every trivial matter, and I have 5.000 things on my mind. If you are capable of governing Krajina, then do it properly, damn it. Don't make me take care of everything. Besides, the civilian government is in your hands." Then, Your Honour, if we can go to the next page, 4, and I suppose you ought to highlight the bit where he -- he -- he, Karadzic, in a fit of irritation, yes. "The point is you keep calling me about every little matter, and that proves you're incompetent." And we'll leave out the swear word at the end. Your Honour, any suggestion that Mr. Brdjanin was not closely involved with Mr. Karadzic, we would say, is not one that is tenable. If we go down to here. Thank you. Brdjanin clearly responding says he's not going to call any more. And then Karadzic says: "No, no. It's not that you can't. Call me about something you cannot resolve. You have all the power in the Krajina, why don't you exercise the power." And then at the bottom of the page this, where he's talking about the police releasing the buses, and he says, Brdjanin says: "I know what we could do. We could dismiss them all, let go of the second floor - as written - and that's it." And Karadzic says: "That's it, Brdo, if Stojan Zupljanin is no good, dismiss him." Now, Your Honour, that goes into line with what we said in our final brief, that this wasn't the rigid hierarchy in the beginnings of the Serbian State in Bosnia that it may well have been in days of peace in Bosnia where the police never did anything but report to their superiors and accept instructions from their superiors. This was a hybrid system. And indeed, one of the witnesses described how the municipal assembly even in the days of peace and before any conflict did have certain powers over the police. But Your Honour, it is clear, we say, on the evidence that there was, as it were, a dual system of control running. Police reporting to the minister of the interior in Pale, but also at the same time taking instructions from the regional authorities. And that was what Karadzic at that stage, even though it may have changed later, intended. He said in one of his speeches in early 1992 "the police must come under the control of the civilian authorities." The Defence say that just means the authorities in Pale; we say not on the evidence of the documents that Your Honours have seen. Your Honour, in July of 1991, Mr. Brdjanin was saying that Mr. Kesic, Your Honour knows was a member of the crisis staff on the intelligence side of the CSB, should be appointed the chief of the State Security Services sector. And then the famous document, P202. And I think it's worth just having that up one more time. "Conclusions reached at the expanded meeting of the centre council held on the 6th of May 1992." And, Your Honour, present is the chiefs, if we can just highlight the first paragraph, of just about every municipality in the ARK, the chiefs of the SJBs, including Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, Petrovac, so on and so forth. And then, Your Honours, if we go to the part which is I think we'll see on -- Your Honour, please, to the second page, or Ms. Gustin, please, to the second page, paragraph 4. All right, could we have it on the ELMO, please. I did ask if we could move to Court I today, Your Honour. Your Honour, "all my orders conveyed orally as well as those I may forward by dispatch must be carried out; they are your law. The chain of command commanding an execution are clearly distinguished in this service." This is important from the point of view of Drljaca as well. "If any one of your staff should refuse to act upon an order, just inform him that he is fired. We have to get rid of the old ideology and concepts not suited to the present moment." All my orders to be carried out. I am -- I was going to say, I am God. But as far as the police are concerned, that was what he was suggesting. And then can we look, please, at paragraph 14. "The chief of the CSB will arrange with the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina to make a decision in accordance with Article 510 of the law of criminal procedure which will entitle the Banja Luka Security Services Centre to acquire all confiscated ownerless property and to sell it and use the profits for equipping of the service." At an early stage, we can see what we on behalf of the Prosecution say was legalised theft, legalised in inverted commas. Finally, if we could turn over to the other side. Your Honours I know you can probably recite this backwards now, but it is worth emphasising. "In all our activities, we are obliged to observe all measures and apply all procedures ordered by the crisis staff of the autonomous region." What on earth, if there was no power for the regional crisis staff to give the police orders or decisions, what was the point of Zupljanin saying this to the chiefs of the local SJBs which came under his command? Yes, thank you, usher. I can have those back. Your Honour, there is also mention of disarmament, but I'm going to deal with that as a separate topic. Now, Your Honour, there are numerous examples of the CSB passing orders down to the local SJBs. Your Honour, I don't think we can work Sanction, so I'll just remind Your Honours of the various... On the 14th of May, and this is P195, Zupljanin sends a dispatch to all the local SJBs ordering "in keeping with the decision of the Autonomous Region of Krajina regarding the surrender of illegally owned weapons and ammunition, public security stations must undertake the following." 31st of July 1992, he forwards a dispatch to all the SJBs in the region ordering the implementation of the ARK crisis staff decision of the 3rd of June which prevented Muslims and Croats leaving the ARK from taking more than 300 deutschemarks with them. And that's P294. I'm just going to check that for a moment. Yes. Then on the 12th of June, so it's a bit out of order, that's why I got a bit confused, Zupljanin forwards to all of the municipal police chiefs the crisis decision of the 10th of June, and I might just put this up because I've got this in hard copy. Could we put this one up. Thanks. This is P240. This is, as you will see, forwarded to the chief of all the public security stations. "Crisis staff of the autonomous regions adopted the following decision, 10th of June," "only children, women, and old people may voluntarily, that is, of their own free will, leave the Autonomous Region of Krajina." The point being that, and some mileage is made of the earlier decisions where they are talking about a voluntary movement of populations. Your Honour, they weren't going to let out of the autonomous region in June anyone who might have taken up arms against them. Women and children can leave voluntarily; everybody else, no. You have to get permission or they're in camps. As we know by the 10th of June in Prijedor, they were. Yes, thank you. And finally, on the 1st of July 1992, they sent out the "dismiss everyone" decision of the 22nd of June, and that's P272. Your Honour, Drljaca on the 5th of July referred to an order of the crisis staff, and that's P1288. Can I just put that up very quickly. And Your Honours will see the first paragraph: "In the wake of the order of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, rifles, pistols, and rounds are being returned." Thank you. That's all I want to do on that one. That's P1288. And very similar in format from Sanski Most, everybody responding to this, five days later -- Your Honour, I'm not going to ask to put it up, but it's the Exhibit P699, from Sanski Most SJB, 10th of July, following the order of the crisis centre, it's called, or translated of the Autonomous Region of Krajina on disarmament these weapons were returned to the army, TO, and SJB units. And it's worth noting the so-called heavily armed Muslim extremists Your Honours saw in the last document, that they managed to recover a couple of automatic rifles, pistols, and 55 rounds. And in Sanski Most, a lot of ammunition and explosions, but not many weapons. Did I say explosions? Explosives. And there's a list breaking down what sort of weapons there were. Your Honour, it's also worth remembering the evidence of the Muslim police officer, Mr. Sadikovic, who, as Your Honours know, was removed and then headed such resistance as there was in Kotor Varos until he was allowed to leave through negotiation. At page 18215, he said: "The police station in Kotor Varos received its instructions from the public security centre in Banja Luka. That was the chain of command and communication." Question: "Now, did the municipal assembly have any authority to issue instructions to the police?" "No, no. Under normal circumstances, that is in peacetime, the interior affairs law, because we have one such, the municipal assembly could propose certain amendments or perhaps if problems arose, if things happened, then they could submit their own proposals, suggestions, and help us to overcome such problems in peacetime. But in wartime, under emergency conditions, of course, the competencies, the terms of reference of the assembly are different than in peacetime so that we were present at meetings when relevant problems were discussed and cooperated and solve all the problems jointly. And we always heeded proposals and suggestions that the assembly had to make. All people employed in the municipal hall in Kotor Varos." Question: "You say in wartime, in emergency conditions. It was different. What happened in respect when the assembly could not sit and its functions were performed by a crisis staff? Could it, the crisis Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. staff, issue such directions to the police?" And he said: "Yes. In such instances, of course, the municipal assembly ceased to function. The crisis staff assumes all its duties, and the crisis staff has more jurisdiction, more competencies over other bodies, that is. And it can have its say in army or police matters, too." And that is an echo of what Mr. Djonlic had to say. Question: "Was the chief of police a member of the crisis staff?" "Yes, ex officio, his office makes him automatically a member of the crisis staff." And Your Honour, later on, and this was after he had been asked questions in cross-examination -- I'm sorry, this was in cross-examination, it was put to him -- he was asked about the law on internal affairs. "Can you tell us" - this is at page 18 - I'm sorry, I should read the whole quote. 18351. "Looking into the law on internal affairs, you learned that the chain of command of the Ministry of the Interior was from the local police, through the regional CSBs, to the MUP in Sarajevo at that time, and that the only civilian authority in the chain of command was at the very top in Sarajevo. Correct?" Answer: "Yes, that's correct. Question: "Now, can you tell us where it is in that law of internal affairs that that situation is any different in wartime or emergency situations? Where in the law on interior affairs does it say civilians can issue orders to the police in an emergency or wartime situation? I think the answer that it doesn't say that. Isn't that true?" Answer: "There may be a misunderstanding here. The law is clear and unambiguous. It only applies to normal situations when there is no war. If there is a state of emergency, a different set of laws apply." And, Your Honour, then in re-examination, that matter was dealt with, and he was shown the document, the law of internal affairs and Article 46. Now, Your Honour, the evidence from BW-1 was different. And indeed, there is again as with so many issues in this case conflicting evidence from the witnesses about this matter. The persons who are -- who gave evidence who are associated with either the regional or the municipal crisis staffs were, with the exception of Mr. Radojko, adamant that there was no power to issue orders to the police. It is suggested that in Mr. Radojko's case, there was a difference because there, there was the changeover from being under the Bihac area CSB to Banja Luka. But Your Honour, if one looks at the documents that we do have from the various crisis staffs, it is littered with orders and instructions to the police, which the evidence shows were carried out. And Mr. Radojko said in terms "it may be couched as an instruction or whatever, but it means it's mandatory or direction." And Your Honour, we suggest that certainly in these times of conflict, the regional and the municipal authorities were able to exercise control and authority over the police. Your Honour, can I come now to the relationship between the regional crisis staff and the military. Can I say straight away, and we've always said this, the regional crisis staff and Mr. Brdjanin, as a civilian at that level, had no de jure authority over the military. That is to say, to give an order to the military as to how to carry out an action. The crisis staff in Kljuc, I think, explained rather well the relationship between the civilian and military at that level. This is Exhibit P208 where they -- and it was dated the 27th of May 1992. And again, I'm sure Your Honours remember this. The relationship of the military authorities to the civilian authorities should be such that the military will execute the orders of the civilian authorities whilst the civilian authorities will not interfere with the way that those orders are carried out. It's the use of the term "order." One has to distinguish between a direction to the military. We need this area cleansed. We need this area attacked because it's full of Muslims who still have weapons. And the order which sends into action the troops. But, Your Honour, it is clear, we suggest, from all the evidence that again, the military don't work in a vacuum. This wasn't a military state. They didn't say "we're going to take control." They said: "We will consult with the political. The political will explain to us what needs to be achieved in a particular area or at a particular time so that the goals which we, the military, have joined in; namely, the establishment of the Serbian State, can be fulfilled." The ARK regional crisis staff did coordinate, the evidence shows, with the armed forces and saw its objectives and its policy being implemented by the military. General Talic was a member of the crisis staff, despite the assertions made by his counsel during the course of the case, in writing and in paper, that he was not a member. There's no doubt he was. People saw him, at least at the first meeting, maybe at one other. His dying declaration, so called, the document that Your Honours I think have admitted as DB300-and-something, 332, which purports to say he wasn't a member of the crisis staff is clearly a lie, even at that late stage. If he wasn't there, you've heard from witnesses that Colonel Vujnovic or another officer was sent to the meetings to take notes and to brief Colonel Talic. Why? If they had no authority and nothing to do with the army? It had, Your Honours, we suggest, the regional crisis staff, an important coordinating function with the 1st Krajina Corps and the other battalions of that corps in the same way as the municipal did with the military and the paramilitary and the TO units. Your Honour, in the excerpt from Mr. Djeric's instructions that we looked at yesterday, it states in terms - thank you, I'm just reminded. Talic's document is DB345. The crisis staff coordinates the functions of authorities in order to ensure the defence of the territories. And you heard from Mr. Brown who explained how the crisis staffs became an important form of the organisation ensuring that coordination took place, bringing together the relevant civilians, military, and police bodies. Your Honour, the control that was exercised by the municipal crisis staffs, which were, we say, subordinated at this stage to the regional crisis staff, that was a strong control over, in particular, the TO units who formed the backbone of the military forces. And it extended well beyond coordination. Your Honour, in April of 1993, the VRS published its report, which Your Honours have seen. I think it's Exhibit P2419. It's a long one, so I'm not going to put it up. On the analysis of the combat readiness and activity of the VRS in 1992. And one of its paragraphs says this: "The Army of the Republika Srpska has grown into the highest strategic organisational formation of the Serbian People in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina capable of realising the strategic and other objectives assigned to it by the Supreme Command and the President of the Republika Srpska as the Supreme Commander." There was the civilian body at the top that did have the direct authority to give orders, real orders, to the military. Your Honour, what is interesting is, as we say, that when they were formed on the 12th of May 1992, the objective of that formation of the VRS was to carry out the objectives of the Serbian People. Your Honour, the -- General Gvero, at the 34th Assembly meeting of the Republika Srpska, amongst other things, saluted the SDS for the initial arming of the Serbian people. This is in Exhibit P355. Your Honour, again, any issue that there seems to have been about the Serbs being armed is not one that seems to have been pursued by the Defence in their final brief. And he explained the strategy of allowing those armed forces to operate outside the formal chain of command. He said: "Nor has anyone rigidly insisted on the military organisation of the operative army since that would surely dangerously impair our front-line strength. For that reason, groups and groupings often of a purely local character which were not suited and were often contrary to an efficient system of warfare command and control, independent and with ideas of their self-sufficiency and their exceptional importance were taken in, armed, and gradually integrated into the army's system of command and control." Your Honour, so much for these paramilitaries operating without any sort of control or allowance from the army. And Your Honours will recall that Lieutenant Milankovic, from being the head of the Wolves of Vucak, taken into the regular VRS troops and decorated at some stage for his sterling assistance to the goals of the Serbian people. Your Honour, part of the control of the exercise which has been well documented in Sanski Most, and in Kljuc and in other places. And Your Honour, as far as Sanski Most is concerned, if one looks just briefly, and perhaps this is the last document before the break, at P637 -- Your Honour, maybe we ought to take the break. I'm told the programme is simply not running at all at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think I'll go into that. I don't know why it's always called "like a dead duck" either. Your Honours, what I was about to deal with was the Sanski Most conclusion of the 21st of May, which is P637, and it gave a whole series of instructions, we say, to the army. It first of all instructed the municipal staff of the Serbian Territorial Defence -- now, that did come directly under the crisis staff -- to find a suitable commander of the civilian defence. The commander of the 6th Brigade, Colonel Basara, and the commander of the Serbian territorial force, Colonel Anicic, and I think Your Honours remember about them, are hereby instructed to protect vital facilities in the town, and so on. Then they give at the end of this document the final deadline for handing in weapons is 2000 hours on the 24th of May. And above that, as far as disarming paramilitary formations in Sanski Most is concerned, Colonel Basara and Colonel Anicic are charged with putting this into practice. Now, Your Honour, this -- there was a plan drafted as a result of this instruction, Your Honour, we say, which led to the attack and the cleansing of Mahala. Your Honours, P638 is the exhibit. And the order given was that the 6th Brigade in coordination with the TO units are ordered to disarm what they call enemy forces. Then, Your Honour, on the 4th of June, the Sanski Most Crisis Staff said that Mr. Rasula, Mr. Vrucinic, the chief of police, and Colonel Anicic in charge of resolving the issue of prisoners and their categorisation and deportation to Manjaca. And it's worth at this stage, Your Honour, and particularly in view of the light of Your Honours' questions about genocide, that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. first category designated is politicians, not fighters; not traitors, but just politicians. And the third category, people unwelcome in Sanski Most Municipality. And the conclusion goes on to say that in view of this, have a talk with Colonel Stevilovic from the 1st Krajina Corps. These camps were run really as a sort of joint -- really a joint enterprise between the civilian, the police, and the military. Whether Manjaca on the face of it was a military camp, and on the face of it Omarska a civilian camp, police camp, but nonetheless, there was this constant coordination between them. Your Honours, again, with the Prijedor Crisis Staff, Your Honours, P1268, there was an intervention platoon ordered to be formed, which dealt, of course, which fought with the military. Your Honour, I'm going to come a little later to Brdjanin's visit as it were to the Kotor Varos area. But, Your Honour, can I remind Your Honours of what Mr. Mayhew said about the sort of control that was being exercised by the military and political forces. He agreed with the assessment of the report that was prepared after the visit at the end of August, beginning of September, which said this: "Despite the existence of warlords, the bulk of the evidence points to the responsibility of acknowledged leaders. The mission believes that in general, leaders exercise effective control over their military and civilian structures. Contrary to what is usually accepted, the so-called uncontrolled elements are marginal. They exist, but their importance has been exaggerated by the various leaders who find them a convenient explanation for numerous barbarities." Your Honour, not only a convenient explanation in 1992, but we suggest a convenient explanation and one that has been attempted to put forward in 19 -- sorry, in 2002 to 2004 as an explanation for these crimes. Your Honour, the municipal crisis staffs published --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Korner. Sorry to interrupt you. Where were you reading from? The reference, I know it's Mr. Mayhew.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the reference I read is from the CSC report which is 1 -- P1617/S217, because it was a Stakic exhibit originally. And Mr. Mayhew agreed that was correct at transcript page 13575. And Your Honour, don't forget that -- sorry, don't forget. I don't mean it quite that way. Can I remind Your Honours that Mr. Mayhew had a lot of experience of the area. He had been there from, I think he told us, the beginning of 1992 before he left, and then came back. Whereas Mr. McLeod came to that particular area for the first time. Your Honour, I'm going to come back to deal with as a discrete topic of the disarmament aspect of matters. But Your Honour, can I deal with some of the other evidence that shows the relationship between the political and the military. Your Honours, the surrender of the resistance fighters in Kotor Varos was achieved by Mr. Kupresanin. Now, this is after I except entirely the period of the crisis staff, and we were then back to the regional authorities as such. He forced the SDA president for the region to take part in the surrender by threatening to have him put in Manjaca. Your Honour, there was undoubtedly a visit by Mr. Kupresanin to Manjaca during the period of this indictment where he went round the buildings telling people that they would be freed. It wasn't true, in most cases. But apparently, he felt no compunction about saying that in a military camp. In addition, and appreciating, of course, Your Honour, that this is in the period after the crisis staff, Mr. Kupresanin removed Mr. Sejmenovic from Omarska. Now, it's not the question on whether that was on the instructions of Karadzic or anyone else, but it does show that the crisis staff, had they cared to use that authority, did have the authority to remove people from camps run by the police and run by the army. Your Honour, in Donji Vakuf, the municipality was run by a military administration until a crisis staff conclusion of the 17th of June 1992 ordered that a civilian government be formed. That's P1725. The military did not tell the ARK Crisis Staff what they could do with that decision; but instead, agreed and yielded control of the municipality to a civilian government. Your Honour, the military removed at the request of the order or discussion or however one puts it, the military removed from its officer corps the Muslims and the Croats. Your Honour, it is suggested --, well, of course, they would do that, wouldn't they, because these men were potentially saboteurs or traitors to the Serbian army. But the fact is that the Serbian army by that stage had already been up and running for well over a month, and although some had been removed the authorities then running the army were perfectly content to keep people like Colonel Selak and Colonel Kranjc in the army. But once the ARK Crisis Staff and indeed the municipalities had expressed their total dissatisfaction with that, the army again, instead of telling the local authorities, the regional authorities what they could do with their view, I'm not going to use the rather vulgar phrase that is sometimes -- is used in these circumstances, did, in fact, comply. Your Honour, the other interesting aspect of the Sanski Unska group, it is said by the Defence that clearly they were renegade, they were going their own way, and as I said yesterday, they felt that the regional crisis staff was not going far enough in achieving the goals of the Serbian people. But what's absolutely fascinating, if they thought it was an ineffective regional crisis staff, then why was it to the regional crisis staff they were going with these demands instead of going directly to General Mladic or to the republican government in Pale? Your Honour, it's a theme that I've already referred to, that there's this, I suppose, still resistance in a way to having the regional authorities imposed upon them. But once imposed, however reluctantly, they accept that this level of authority does have the power. Now, Your Honours, finally can I deal with one last series on this set of documents. In a conclusion dated the 18th of May 1992, the ARK Crisis Staff issued the specific directive that illegally obtained weapons will be taken away by members of the civilian and military police. That is on Exhibit P227. It's the 18th of May. We're just going to see if we can find it. No. Maybe. Now, Your Honour, the disarmament process in Kljuc demonstrates one of the many examples which confirm that the ARK decision was acted upon by the military and the police. On the 28th of May of 1992, the Kljuc Crisis Staff at 0800 hours, 8.00 in the morning, held a meeting, and they ordered, and this is Exhibit P196, that citizens who own illegally acquired weapons, and we say that means only Muslims and Croats on the evidence, must hand them in between 1200 and 1400 hours with the accompanying dire warning: "otherwise vigorous measures will be implemented to carry out disarmament which could have disastrous consequences for the security of both people and property." That's P921. On that same day, the command of the 1st Infantry Brigade of the 1st Krajina Corps reported, and this is P924, "because of the situation in Kljuc, the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Infantry Brigade was made fully combat ready as ordered. If the Muslims - Muslims, not people illegally in possession of weapons, Serbian paramilitaries or whatever - do not surrender their weapons by the 27th of May at 1200 hours the battalion will carry out" - a wonderful phrase - "a mopping up operation." The very next day, the 29th of May, General Talic reported to the Main Staff of the VRS. This is in P654. There is still some weak resistance to the confiscation of weapons in the wider area of Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc. And he further reported under the heading"combat dispositions of the units" that "cooperation with the MUP in mopping up the terrain and confiscating weapons from illegal formations in the area of Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc continues." And Your Honours know from the evidence exactly what happened in Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc. Now, Your Honour, those are just some of the issues and some of the documents which we have gone into at far greater length in the written final brief that show, we say, the authority, the coordination between the regional authorities, the crisis staff, the police, and the army. Your Honour, can I now move to, as it were, a quick canter through some of the evidence of the implementation of the criminal plan in the autonomous region. Your Honour, the events which took place in the municipalities, in particular, of the variant B type, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, Kotor Varos, all of them reveal an identical pattern of events which led directly to the commission of the crimes. Your Honour, in our original pre-trial brief, we said this: "The events which took place were not spontaneous or haphazard, but were part of a carefully planned and executed enterprise. It is the case for the Prosecution that the ferocity of the methods used by death or deportation of the non-Serbs and all vestiges of their existence, culture, and religion indicate an intention which it is submitted was to destroy in whole or in part the Muslim and Croat peoples living in the ARK." "It is," we said, "the Prosecution's case that the crimes committed in the various municipalities did in some areas result in the destruction of almost all the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat peoples who had resided there." And Your Honour, tomorrow we'll remind Your Honours of what the evidence was. "The methodical, systematic, widespread and repetitive nature of the crimes which included many large-scale killings leads to the irresistible conclusion, we said then, that what was planned and intended was the destruction of these peoples because of their ethnicity." Your Honours, that's what we said we hoped to prove. Your Honour, we would submit now that on the evidence, we have proved those allegations because taking that evidence in its most summary form, the pattern of events in the municipalities was as follows: It started really in most places with persecutions through the dismissals of Muslims and Croats, a persecution which continued steadily and increasing in its ferocity throughout the period of the indictment. Contrary to the assertions made by the Defence in their final trial brief, these dismissals did not just affect those who occupied jobs which could be said to be sensitive in terms of the security of the Serbian State. One of the matters they rely on, the Geneva Conventions which says that in times of emergency, you can dismiss people. But Your Honour, they didn't just dismiss people who were in charge of companies that were important for production or in the telegraph offices. They dismissed everybody who was a Muslim or nearly everybody who was a Muslim or a Croat. Factory workers. Road workers. Your Honours have heard a myriad of description of those who were actually dismissed, and I remind Your Honour this morning of some of the evidence of Petrovac. A company who had been told to lay people off because they were Muslim or Croat. In any event, Your Honour, after being dismissed, those not imprisoned or expelled were, in fact, still forced to work under work obligation. They just didn't get paid for it. They didn't have any job security. They didn't have any homes. They were attached to the work. Would Your Honour forgive me a moment. Your Honour, I think it's worth just playing what Mr. Brdjanin himself said about that, which we have on video. It was a video clearly reported -- it was a report around the discovery of the camps in August. We're just going to see if we can play it. Yes, it's going to be in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. small.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "No place in leading jobs for people who are not loyal to Serb policies." But as the reporter himself said, by 1992, or August of 1992, nearly all persons had been sacked. Now, Your Honour, the disarmament order which as I say I'm going to come back to is, again, one that has been the subject of dispute. It is alleged that the order was applicable to all, Serbs, Muslims, and Croats alike. Your Honours have heard from many Muslims about the disarmament and fewer Croats. Your Honours, I would ask Your Honours to look at what BT-95 had to say in respect of Teslic. That's at transcript page number 19532 to 3. Colonel Sajic said this, or this was what he said in interview of which he was reminded. "During your interview with us, you talked honestly about who was disarmed. You were asked talking about the order on mobilisation and disarmament, but the effect was this, wasn't it, that it was only the Muslims and Croats who were having their weapons removed from them?" And his answer, or as it was put in the transcript, your answer: "Mainly, you can't it was a hundred per cent like that. But this statement can stand." That's at T23683. Your Honour, when one looks at that page, he went on to explain how we had a Muslim friend who wanted to keep his weapon, but even with his intervention, the weapon was removed. Your Honour, as far as Sanski Most is concerned, would Your Honours care, please, to look when you consider the matter at BT-104, transcript page 18513. Now, Your Honour, the Defence in their response at page 4 are still trying, we say valiantly, to persuade this Trial Chamber that you should reject the compelling evidence that disarmament was only enforced against the Muslims and Croats. And at page 4, they say this: "There simply was no order of the ARK Crisis Staff aimed solely at non-Serbs in possession of weapons." And dealing with one of our cites, I think that was BT-104, the one I've just put before Your Honour. "The cite is to the unique situation in Sanski Most, a renegade municipality." Your Honours, this is simply on the evidence not right. Your Honour, of course not one of the orders says from the ARK Crisis Staff "disarm by the 11th of May or the 14th of May" or whatever, it is only "only Muslims and Croats." But that is the effect of the enforcement. And Your Honour, there are five ARK Crisis Staff conclusions between the 8th and the 18th of May, averaging one every two days, which demand that weapons be surrendered. And the language used includes, for the 14th of May, "the strictest sanctions would be applied" I'm sorry, for the 8th of May -- would be applied to those who refused. And on the 14th of May: "Severe sanction would be imposed on those who ignore the call of the crisis staff." Now, Your Honour, it wasn't just that Brdjanin as president of the ARK Crisis Staff, his signature was on the bottom of these decisions, he made public statements throwing his weight behind those decisions and demanding that weapons be surrendered. On the 9th of May, reported in Oslobodjenje, that's P180, under the title "weapons must be returned," "members of paramilitary units and individuals from the autonomous region Bosanska Krajina must return all weapons and other means of combat in their illegal possession by the 11th of May" stated today, Radoslav Brdjanin, the commander of the war staff of Bosanska Krajina. Same day, in Glas, I think probably the same press conference, P181. It's under the title "no more beating under around the bush." "Speaking about the order disarm individuals and illegal formations, Brdjanin warned that he expected most of them to return their weapons to the municipal staffs of the TO by the 11th of May, adding that weapons would be taken by force by those who refused to do so." Your Honour, the suggestion that Mr. Brdjanin was not wholeheartedly behind and involved in the force behind the Autonomous Region of Krajina is, we say, completely misconceived. Your Honour, the order from the CSB that we just looked at included the part relating to disarmament with regard to decisions -- with regard to disarmament when the deadline for weapons surrender expires on the 11th of May, we should take no action until the crisis staff makes the relevant decisions. And they made a relevant decision. They extended the deadlines. And Your Honour, when Mr. Sajic dealt with that passage, he agreed that the crisis staff was in control of what happened. Your Honour, one can see that at transcript page 23720 to 21. I'm summarising, because it was quite a lengthy passage. Now, Your Honour, those decisions were vital because they served, we say, as the pretext for the attacks on the Muslim and Croat villages. Your Honour has heard testimony, and again, I'd invite you to look at BT-104 at page 18514, that the pretext of disarmament was used for the excuse to attack and cleanse the Muslim neighbourhood of Mahala in Sanski Most. It was the achievement of the strategic goal number 1. The accused and the ARK Crisis Staff, in fact, provided a ready-made justification for the attacks by the military and police, which they said would be the people carrying out the disarmament operation. And as we say, the contention that these apply to anyone other than Muslims and Croats is wrong. The -- in the -- on May the 12th, as we reminded you yesterday, Mr. Vjestica was already talking about that disarmament process going on in Bosanski Novi, and it was about to start in Sanski Most. And the reports from the Sanski Most police, P680 and P - I'm sorry, I've lost my note here - but certainly P680 shows that Serbian Army units and Territorial Defence units and the SJB have for some time been disarming paramilitary Muslim and Croatian formations. 15th of June, that is. Your Honour, in Hambarine, in Prijedor -- sorry, I've just lost my place in my note for a moment. Yes, Your Honour, in Hambarine, the incident involving the checkpoint was used, we say, as the pretext. In Kljuc, the incident around the Pudin Han area in which Omer Filipovic became involved. All of these small incidents, we say, were then used -- the incidents ariding -- arising, I'm sorry, as a result of the disarmament process when Muslims were actually saying "we know what's going to happen. We're not going to hand over our arms," the forces, the overwhelming forces of the Serbian government was sent in. Your Honour, in Sanski Most, amongst the crisis staff there, there was a person who was then involved in the killings, Mr. Danilusko Kajtez. The SOS in Sanski Most was involved in that. And he then became a member of the 6th Krajina Brigade under Colonel Basara. I'm sorry, I said he was a member of the crisis staff. He was a member of the SOS. And I'm sorry, it's my fault. He was a member of the crisis staff -- now, I'm doing it again. He was a member of the SOS in Sanski Most. There was a reference to him in Rasula's diary entry for the 6th of May, which is P759. Now, Your Honour, as records other areas, in Lisnija, the population was attacked by the members of, I think, the VRS. And there's a report from General Talic, P657, that talks about the expelling of the Muslim population in the area of Lisnija. Lisnija was, in fact, attacked. Your Honour, those attacks were carried out sometimes with warnings, sometimes without any warning whatsoever. Brisevo was attacked twice. That's the evidence of Mr. Atlija. The first attack was in May, and that's at transcript page 1193. It was put to him, because he had given evidence in Stakic, and his transcript was being gone through: "You described at some length the actual attack on Brisevo." I'm sorry, I'm doing the attack in July. "Which began at half past 3.00 on the 24th of July. Is that right?" "It is." "And this is an attack which took place without any warning whatsoever?" "That's right." Brisevo was a Croat village. By July of 1992, the Prijedor area, municipality, was under the complete control of the Serbian forces. Having been attacked in May, it's then attacked again in July. It is filled with women and children. It is shelled. It is then attacked, looted, and indeed I think no longer exists as a village. Your Honour, that happened not just there but in villages and areas all over the Autonomous Region of Krajina. After the shelling took place, troops entered, killings took place of unarmed survivors of the shellings, homes were looted. They were set on fire. And mosques and churches were destroyed. In a minute, we're going to look at a videoclip about mosques and churches, but it is suggested that the Prosecution have failed to prove that these mosques and churches were not being used for military purposes. Leaving aside the fact that not to one single witness was it ever suggested that they were being used for military purposes, accepting the Defence don't have to put things that aren't part of their case. Your Honours, the overwhelming descriptions that you have had of how these mosques were destroyed and the churches as well has been through shelling, through deliberate destruction once troops are in the village. The public prosecutor in Teslic had no doubt about it. He sent in a report saying the destruction of these mosques and churches are a war crime. No, as I say, not even no suggestion, it's clear from the evidence that Your Honours have heard that the mosques were not being used for any kind of military purpose. Your Honour, destruction of cultural, religious edifices and the like is not in itself genocide. The authorities are quite clear on that. But it can be used as a pointer to the intent of those involved to destroy the Muslims and Croat peoples. And Your Honour, we would suggest that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was addressed yesterday in the Krstic as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely right, Your Honour. And I think they have exactly dealt with that. Your Honour, I was going to deal with that as a matter. Your Honour, those not killed during or immediately after the attacks were rounded up. The men, and in some cases the women, were taken to camps where killings and ill treatment occurred. In the most part, the women and children were separated, and they were taken, to begin with, to temporary camps. In many of those temporary camps, the women were raped. After that, they were deported using the word in its most loose frame, as opposed to the difference between deportation and forcible transfer. Your Honour, those Muslims and Croats not in areas where the major attacks took place were forced out, often in huge convoys, with the totally unwilling cooperation of the humanitarian organisations. But we could simply see, and this is particularly true of the evidence Your Honours heard in respect of Bosanski Novi and Bosanski Petrovac, that if they did not assist, these Muslims were at risk of being killed or put into camps. Your Honour, in more than one municipality, but in particular, in Petrovac, witnesses agreed the Muslims posed no serious threat. Mr. Radojko said that, or any threat at all, at transcript page 20069. In Prijedor, Your Honour, there was a document produced, and I'm going to put it up. It's P1379. Sorry, Your Honour, I'm just going to find it for a moment. Your Honour, again, this was a document that I... Your Honour, this was a security assessment for the Prijedor Municipality, and it's dated the 23rd of October 1992. Can we put page 1 on the ELMO. Can we turn over to the next page, please. Your Honour, now this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is a description in October of what happened earlier on. "The situation in the Prijedor Municipality started deteriorating in May 1992." Tension could be felt. Relations between the ethnic groups became very tense. The national division reached its climax in armed conflicts between the Serbian people which had taken power and Muslim and Croatian extremists on the other. From then until today, the consequences of these conflicts can be felt everywhere. Dozens of villages have been almost completely destroyed and left uninhabited. And Your Honours can see the list, or partly destroyed. This destruction saw the beginnings of the mass exodus of both Muslims and Croats. According to estimates, roughly, and this is October, by October 1992, 38.000 Muslim and Croat citizens have left the Municipality of Prijedor so far. How they left. As they people left, there began a massive looting of their property which was left entirely unguarded by either the owners or the municipal authorities. Then we can move the page up slightly. Then it deals with the worry that they may get involved. I would say that was probably more than a worry. Once they had left in hostile activities against the Republika Srpska. The remainder of the Muslim and Croat population, at least, the more extreme ones amongst them, must be treated with extreme caution as they refuse to accept the present situation. The entire period is characterised by the blowing up and destruction of buildings owned by Muslims and Croats, as well as of places of worship. This represents a direct threat to the life and property of all the citizens of the municipality. The harassment of other nationality by individuals wearing military uniform is also evident. Such individuals are increasingly becoming a threat to all the other citizens of the Municipality of Prijedor. And again, there's that corollary of what happened in Teslic with the Mice. Some terrorised Serbs. And the military police in the town are doing almost nothing about this problem. Thank you. I think I did say the exhibit number, but if I haven't, Your Honour, it's -- yes, I thought I had. Your Honour, as well as being, as we saw from that report, deported, looted, the municipalities then engaged in -- with the -- through the, effectively the orders again of the crisis staff in legalised theft by insisting that people who were leaving "voluntarily" couldn't take more than 300 marks with them. And that they had to sign over, if they were any owners of property, they had to sign over that property to the Municipality. Your Honours, it's all too easy to forget as I have been going on for the last day, and effectively for the last few months, what we're talking about here. We're not talking about names on a piece of paper, names of villages, but of real, live people, some of them from whom Your Honours have heard. And, Your Honours, these cases are brought for a number of reasons. The first is, and the most important, that if people commit criminal offences, they should be brought to book for them. But as I think Your Honours have said on a number of occasions, it's also to try and achieve some kind of peace and reconciliation in Bosnia. But of course, it's also right that the victims of these crimes, and we say in this case, these undisputed crimes, are heard. And Your Honour, I think it's right to remind Your Honours just very shortly, although one clip is a bit longer than normal, but it's important that Your Honours hear it, and that is of some of the evidence that we've heard about the attacks and the killings and the beatings. And Your Honours, I want to start with the evidence of Dr. Merdzanic about the attack on Kozarac, which is Exhibit P...
